## Question 1

Find the complete set of values of $k$ for which the line $y=x-2$ crosses or touches the curve
$y=x^{2}+kx+2$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $-1\leq k\leq 3$ &nbsp; **B** $-3\leq k\leq 5$ &nbsp; **C** $-4\leq k\leq 4$ &nbsp;
**D** $k\leq-1$ or $k\geq3$ &nbsp; **E** $k\leq-3$ or $k\geq5$ &nbsp; **F** $k\leq-4$ or $k\geq4$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**E.** "Crosses **or** touches" means the line and curve meet — the simultaneous equations have **at least one
real solution**. Set them equal:
$$x^{2}+kx+2=x-2\;\Longrightarrow\;x^{2}+(k-1)x+4=0.$$
This quadratic in $x$ has a real root exactly when its discriminant is $\geq0$:
$$(k-1)^{2}-4(1)(4)\geq0\;\Longrightarrow\;(k-1)^{2}\geq16\;\Longrightarrow\;k-1\leq-4\ \text{or}\ k-1\geq4.$$
Hence $k\leq-3$ or $k\geq5$.

*The trap is answering with the "between" interval (option B) — that is the range where the line **misses**
the curve. "$\geq0$" for "meets" always gives the **outside** region.*

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-6,6,400)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8,3.4))
for k,c in [(-3,'#2b6cb0'),(5,'#dd6b20')]:
    ax.plot(x,x**2+k*x+2,color=c,lw=1.8,label=f'$k={k}$ (tangent)')
ax.plot(x,x-2,'k--',lw=1.3,label='$y=x-2$')
ax.set_ylim(-8,14); ax.axhline(0,color='0.7',lw=.6); ax.axvline(0,color='0.7',lw=.6)
ax.legend(fontsize=8,loc='upper center'); ax.set_title('Boundary cases $k=-3$ and $k=5$: line is tangent',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

## Question 2

Given that $\tan\theta=2$ and $180^\circ<\theta<360^\circ$, find the value of $\cos\theta$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\sqrt3$ &nbsp; **B** $-\sqrt3$ &nbsp; **C** $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ &nbsp;
**D** $-\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ &nbsp; **E** $\dfrac{\sqrt5}{5}$ &nbsp; **F** $-\dfrac{\sqrt5}{5}$ &nbsp;
**G** $\dfrac{2\sqrt5}{5}$ &nbsp; **H** $-\dfrac{2\sqrt5}{5}$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**F.** $\tan\theta=2>0$ happens in the **first** and **third** quadrants. The range $180^\circ<\theta<360^\circ$
rules out the first quadrant, so $\theta$ is in the **third quadrant**, where $\cos\theta<0$.

Build a right triangle with opposite $=2$, adjacent $=1$, so hypotenuse $=\sqrt{1^{2}+2^{2}}=\sqrt5$. Then
$\lvert\cos\theta\rvert=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt5}$, and the third-quadrant sign makes it **negative**:
$$\cos\theta=-\frac{1}{\sqrt5}=-\frac{\sqrt5}{5}.$$

*The whole question turns on the sign. Reading "$\tan\theta>0$" straight to the acute answer $+\tfrac{\sqrt5}{5}$
(option E) forgets that the given range forces the third quadrant.*
:::

## Question 3

A student claims: *for all integers $n$, the expression $4\!\left(\dfrac{9n+1}{2}-\dfrac{3n-1}{2}\right)$ is
divisible by $3$.* The argument runs:

$$\begin{aligned}
4\!\left(\tfrac{9n+1}{2}-\tfrac{3n-1}{2}\right)&=2\!\left(2\!\left(\tfrac{9n+1}{2}-\tfrac{3n-1}{2}\right)\right) &&\text{(I)}\\
&=2(9n+1-3n-1) &&\text{(II)}\\
&=2(6n) &&\text{(III)}\\
&=12n &&\text{(IV)}\\
&=3(4n)\ \text{— always a multiple of }3 &&\text{(V, VI)}
\end{aligned}$$

Which one is true — is it correct, or where is the first error?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** correct &nbsp; **B** first error line (I) &nbsp; **C** first error line (II) &nbsp;
**D** line (III) &nbsp; **E** line (IV) &nbsp; **F** line (V) &nbsp; **G** line (VI)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**C.** Line (I) is fine ($4X=2(2X)$). The error is at **line (II)**: cancelling the two $\tfrac12$'s should
give $2\big((9n+1)-(3n-1)\big)$, and the **minus in front of the bracket** must flip *both* terms:
$$2\big(9n+1-(3n-1)\big)=2(9n+1-3n+1)=2(6n+2)=12n+4.$$
The student wrote "$-3n-1$" instead of "$-3n+1$", dropping the sign on the second term.

**The claim is actually false.** The true value is $4(3n+1)=12n+4$, which leaves remainder $1$ on division by
$3$. The bogus "$12n$" at line (IV) is a *consequence* of the sign slip at (II).

*Toolkit link (S7): the first error is the earliest line that fails — not the line where the answer finally
looks wrong. Trace the algebra top-down and stop at the first broken step.*
:::

## Question 4

Consider the statement: *every positive integer $N$ greater than $6$ can be written as the sum of two
non-prime integers that are greater than $1$.* Which of the following is/are **counterexample(s)**?

$$\text{I}\quad N=5 \qquad \text{II}\quad N=7 \qquad \text{III}\quad N=9$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II &nbsp; **F** I and III &nbsp; **G** II and III &nbsp; **H** I, II and III

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**G.** A counterexample must **satisfy the hypothesis** ($N>6$) and **fail the conclusion**.

- **I ($N=5$):** $5$ is not greater than $6$, so it does not even enter the statement — **not a counterexample**.
- **II ($N=7$):** the non-primes greater than $1$ up to $7$ are $\{4,6\}$. The only way to reach $7$ using a
  value from this set is $4+3$, but $3$ is prime. So $7$ **cannot** be written as required — a genuine
  counterexample.
- **III ($N=9$):** the usable non-primes are $\{4,6,8\}$. Pairs summing to $9$: $4+5$ ($5$ prime), $6+3$ ($3$
  prime), $8+1$ ($1$ not allowed). None work — also a counterexample.

So II and III only.

*Toolkit link (S5): to disprove a "for all", one valid case is enough — but the case must **obey the
hypothesis**. $N=5$ is the classic decoy that fails the domain, not the conclusion.*
:::

## Question 5

Which one of the following shows the graph of $\displaystyle y=\frac{2^{x}}{1+2^{x}}$? (Dotted lines indicate
asymptotes.)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** increasing S-curve, top asymptote &nbsp; **B** increasing, no upper asymptote &nbsp;
**C** decreasing, low asymptote &nbsp; **D** decreasing S-curve, top asymptote &nbsp;
**E** decreasing, no asymptote &nbsp; **F** decreasing, low asymptote

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**A.** Read off the **behaviour at the two ends** and the **middle value**:

- As $x\to-\infty$: $2^{x}\to0$, so $y\to\dfrac{0}{1+0}=0$ — a horizontal asymptote $y=0$ below.
- As $x\to+\infty$: divide top and bottom by $2^{x}$ to get $y=\dfrac{1}{2^{-x}+1}\to\dfrac{1}{0+1}=1$ — a
  horizontal asymptote $y=1$ above.
- At $x=0$: $y=\dfrac{1}{1+1}=\tfrac12$, and $y$ is **increasing** throughout (numerator grows faster than the
  "$+1$" drag).

So the graph is an increasing S-curve rising from $0$ to $1$ — option **A**.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x=np.linspace(-6,6,400); y=2.0**x/(1+2.0**x)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(4.8,3.2))
ax.plot(x,y,color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
ax.axhline(0,color='crimson',ls=':',lw=1.2); ax.axhline(1,color='crimson',ls=':',lw=1.2)
ax.axvline(0,color='0.7',lw=.6)
ax.plot(0,0.5,'o',color='#dd6b20'); ax.annotate('$(0,\\frac{1}{2})$',(0.2,0.52),fontsize=9)
ax.set_ylim(-0.15,1.15); ax.set_title('$y=2^x/(1+2^x)$: rises from $0$ to $1$',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

## Question 6

The function $\mathrm f(x)$ is defined for all real $x$. Which conditions on $\mathrm f$ is/are **necessary**
to ensure that $\displaystyle\int_{-5}^{0}\mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx=\int_{0}^{5}\mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx$?

$$\text{I}\ \ \mathrm f(x)=\mathrm f(-x)\qquad \text{II}\ \ \mathrm f(x)=c\ (\text{constant})\qquad
\text{III}\ \ \mathrm f(x)=-\mathrm f(-x)$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II &nbsp; **F** I and III &nbsp; **G** II and III &nbsp; **H** I, II and III

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**A.** "**Necessary**" reverses the arrow: a condition is necessary only if the integral identity **forces**
it. So test each by asking *"can the identity hold while this condition fails?"*

- **I (even):** an even function does give equal halves — but that is **sufficient, not necessary**. Plenty of
  non-even functions also balance the two halves.
- **II (constant):** a constant gives $5c=5c$ — again sufficient, not necessary.
- **III (odd):** an odd function gives $\int_{-5}^{0}=-\int_{0}^{5}$, so the identity would force
  $\int_{0}^{5}\mathrm f=0$ — it usually **fails**, so it is certainly not forced.

A concrete balancer that is none of I, II, III: any $\mathrm f$ that is even on $[-5,5]$ but... simpler, take
$\mathrm f$ built so both halves equal (say) $3$ without symmetry — e.g. two different bumps of equal area.
The identity holds, yet every one of I–III is false. Hence **none** is necessary.

*Toolkit link (S3): sufficient = "condition $\Rightarrow$ result"; necessary = "result $\Rightarrow$
condition". Here each option is a sufficient recipe, and none is squeezed out by the result.*
:::

## Question 7

$PQRS$ is a **parallelogram** labelled anticlockwise. Which of the conditions is/are individually
**sufficient** for $PQRS$ to be a **square**?

$$\text{I}\ \ \lvert PQ\rvert=\lvert QR\rvert\qquad \text{II}\ \ PR\perp QS\qquad \text{III}\ \ \angle PQR=\angle QRS$$

The options A–H give every yes/no pattern for (I sufficient, II sufficient, III sufficient).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**H** (no, no, no). In a parallelogram each condition upgrades the shape by **one** property, and a square
needs **two** (equal sides *and* right angles). One alone is never enough:

- **I — adjacent sides equal:** a parallelogram with equal adjacent sides is a **rhombus**. Its angles need
  not be $90^\circ$ — not sufficient.
- **II — diagonals perpendicular:** in a parallelogram, perpendicular diagonals also give exactly a
  **rhombus**, not a square — not sufficient.
- **III — $\angle PQR=\angle QRS$:** consecutive angles of a parallelogram are supplementary, so if they are
  *equal* each is $90^\circ$: a **rectangle**. The sides need not be equal — not sufficient.

Each produces "rhombus **or** rectangle", never forced all the way to a square. So all three are "no" — **H**.

*Toolkit link (S3): sufficient means the condition alone **guarantees** the target. A near-miss (rhombus /
rectangle) is a counterexample to sufficiency.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}

## Question 8

A student decides whether $(*)$ *for all real $a,b$, $\lvert a+b\rvert<\lvert a\rvert+\lvert b\rvert$* is true
or false, and writes:

> $(*)$ is **false**. A counterexample is $a=3,b=4$, as $\lvert3+4\rvert=7$ and $\lvert3\rvert+\lvert4\rvert=7$,
> but "$7<7$" is false.

Which best describes the proof?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $(*)$ true, proof not correct &nbsp; **B** $(*)$ false, counterexample not valid &nbsp;
**C** $(*)$ false, but must give **all** failing $a,b$ &nbsp; **D** $(*)$ false, should have used $\leq$ &nbsp;
**E** $(*)$ false, proof fully correct

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**E.** Check the three things a disproof needs.

1. **Is $(*)$ really false?** When $a,b$ have the **same sign** (or either is $0$), $\lvert a+b\rvert=\lvert
   a\rvert+\lvert b\rvert$, so the *strict* "$<$" fails. $(*)$ is indeed false. (The true statement is the
   triangle inequality with "$\leq$".)
2. **Is one counterexample enough?** Yes — a single case defeats a "for all" claim; there is no need to list
   every failure (so C is wrong).
3. **Is the given case valid?** At $a=3,b=4$ both sides equal $7$, so "$7<7$" is false there — a genuine
   counterexample.

Statement false, proof complete and correct — **E**. (D misreads the task: the student was asked to judge
*this* statement, not to fix it.)

*Toolkit link (S7): to disprove "$<$ for all", you only need one place where "$<$" fails — and equality counts
as a failure of strict inequality.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}

## Question 9

A student wants to evaluate $\mathrm f(x)=x\sin x$ with $x$ in **radians**, but the calculator only works in
**degrees**. What can be typed to evaluate $\mathrm f(4)$ correctly?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $(\pi\times4\div180)\times\sin(4)$ &nbsp; **B** $(\pi\times4\div180)\times\sin(\pi\times4\div180)$ &nbsp;
**C** $4\times\sin(\pi\times4\div180)$ &nbsp; **D** $(180\times4\div\pi)\times\sin(4)$ &nbsp;
**E** $(180\times4\div\pi)\times\sin(180\times4\div\pi)$ &nbsp; **F** $4\times\sin(180\times4\div\pi)$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**F.** Split $\mathrm f(4)=4\times\sin(4\ \text{radians})$ into its two factors and fix only what the
calculator gets wrong.

- The **leading $x=4$** is just the number $4$ — a radian *measure* is a pure number, so it stays as `4`.
- The **angle inside $\sin$** must be $4$ **radians**. A degrees calculator needs that same angle re-expressed
  in degrees: $4\ \text{rad}=4\times\dfrac{180}{\pi}\ \text{degrees}=(180\times4\div\pi)^\circ$.

So type $4\times\sin(180\times4\div\pi)$ — option **F**.

*The decoys go the wrong way: multiplying by $\pi/180$ converts degrees $\to$ radians, but the calculator
already reads its input as degrees, so you must convert the radian angle **into** degrees ($\times180/\pi$),
and only inside the $\sin$.*
:::

## Question 10

The real numbers $a,b,c,d$ satisfy both $0<a+b<c+d$ and $0<a+c<b+d$. Which inequalities **must** be true?

$$\text{I}\ \ a<d\qquad \text{II}\ \ b<c\qquad \text{III}\ \ a+b+c+d>0$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II &nbsp; **F** I and III &nbsp; **G** II and III &nbsp; **H** I, II and III

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**F.** Work from the two given inequalities.

- **I ($a<d$): true.** **Add** the two given inequalities (adding same-direction inequalities is always
  legal): $(a+b)+(a+c)<(c+d)+(b+d)$, i.e. $2a+b+c<b+c+2d$, so $2a<2d$ and $a<d$. ✔
- **III ($a+b+c+d>0$): true.** From $0<a+b<c+d$ we get $a+b>0$ *and* $c+d>a+b>0$, so both halves are positive
  and their sum is positive. ✔
- **II ($b<c$): not forced.** You cannot **subtract** inequalities. Counterexample $a=0,b=3,c=2,d=2$: then
  $a+b=3<c+d=4$ ✔ and $a+c=2<b+d=5$ ✔, yet $b=3>c=2$. ✘

So I and III must hold, II need not — **F**.

*Toolkit link (S3): you may **add** two "$<$"s but never **subtract** them. Statement II is the trap that
tempts an illegal subtraction.*
:::

::: {.workspace style="min-height:3cm"}

## Question 11

A square spiral is drawn from the origin and continues indefinitely, turning through the lattice points as
shown in the paper. Which one of these points is **not** on the spiral?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $(99,100)$ &nbsp; **B** $(99,-100)$ &nbsp; **C** $(-99,100)$ &nbsp; **D** $(-99,-100)$ &nbsp;
**E** $(100,99)$ &nbsp; **F** $(100,-99)$ &nbsp; **G** $(-100,99)$ &nbsp; **H** $(-100,-99)$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**G.** Describe the four families of straight edges by the level they sit on (read off the small picture, then
continued):

| Edge | Line | Range it covers |
|---|---|---|
| right verticals | $x=2k$ | $-2k\leq y\leq 2k$ |
| top horizontals | $y=2k$ | $-2k-2\leq x\leq 2k$ |
| left verticals | $x=-2k$ | $-2k\leq y\leq 2k-2$ |
| bottom horizontals | $y=-2k$ | $-2k\leq x\leq 2k$ |

The key asymmetry: a **left vertical** $x=-2k$ stops **two short of the top**, at $y=2k-2$, because the
horizontal above it starts one column further left (at $x=-2k-2$). Now test the candidates with $k=50$:

- $(100,\pm99)$ sit on the right vertical $x=100$ ($-100\leq y\leq100$) — on the spiral. So do the four corner
  points $(\pm99,\pm100)$ on the top/bottom horizontals $y=\pm100$.
- $(-100,-99)$ sits on the left vertical $x=-100$, which runs $-100\leq y\leq 98$ — on the spiral.
- $(-100,99)$: the same left vertical only reaches $y=98$, so $y=99$ is **just above where the spiral has
  already turned left**. Not on the spiral.

Hence **G**.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
# build the spiral outward as a polyline through its corners
pts=[(0,0)]
x=y=0; step=2; d=0  # directions: right, up, left, down (anticlockwise)
dirs=[(1,0),(0,1),(-1,0),(0,-1)]
for i in range(1,9):
    # lengths grow 2,2,4,4,6,6,... producing the observed corners
    L=2*((i+1)//2)
    dx,dy=dirs[d]; x+=dx*L; y+=dy*L; pts.append((x,y)); d=(d+1)%4
xs,ys=zip(*pts)
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(4.4,4.4))
ax.plot(xs,ys,color='#2b6cb0',lw=2)
ax.set_xlim(-9,9); ax.set_ylim(-9,9); ax.set_aspect('equal')
ax.axhline(0,color='0.8',lw=.6); ax.axvline(0,color='0.8',lw=.6)
ax.set_title('The square spiral (first few turns)',fontsize=9)
ax.grid(True,color='0.9',lw=.5); plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

## Question 12

Which one of **A–F** correctly completes: *"Given $a<b$ and $\mathrm f(x)>0$ for all $x$ with $a<x<b$, the
trapezium rule produces an **overestimate** for $\displaystyle\int_a^b\mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx$ …"*

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** *if* $\mathrm f'>0$ and $\mathrm f''<0$ &nbsp; **B** *only if* $\mathrm f'>0$ and $\mathrm f''<0$ &nbsp;
**C** *iff* $\mathrm f'>0$ and $\mathrm f''<0$ &nbsp; **D** *if* $\mathrm f'<0$ and $\mathrm f''>0$ &nbsp;
**E** *only if* $\mathrm f'<0$ and $\mathrm f''>0$ &nbsp; **F** *iff* $\mathrm f'<0$ and $\mathrm f''>0$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**D.** The geometry first: the trapezium rule joins points on the curve by **straight chords**. A chord lies
**above** a curve that bends upward, so the rule **overestimates exactly when the curve is convex**, i.e.
when $\mathrm f''(x)>0$ — regardless of whether $\mathrm f$ is increasing or decreasing.

Now weigh *if* / *only if* / *iff*:

- **D — "*if* $\mathrm f'<0$ and $\mathrm f''>0$":** $\mathrm f''>0$ already guarantees an overestimate, so
  this is a **true (sufficient) implication**. ✔
- **F — "*iff*":** false, because overestimate does **not** require $\mathrm f'<0$; a convex **increasing**
  function ($\mathrm f'>0,\ \mathrm f''>0$) also overestimates.
- **E — "*only if*":** false for the same reason (overestimate does not force $\mathrm f'<0$).
- **A, B, C** all use $\mathrm f''<0$ (concave), which makes the rule **under**estimate — the wrong direction.

So the only correct completion is the one-way "if" in **D**.

*Toolkit link (S2): "$P$ if $Q$" means $Q\Rightarrow P$; "$P$ only if $Q$" means $P\Rightarrow Q$; "iff" is
both. A true one-way "if" with an over-strong extra hypothesis ($\mathrm f'<0$) is still true.*
:::

## Question 13

$\mathrm f(x)$ is a function for which
$$\int_{0}^{3}\big(\mathrm f(x)\big)^{2}\,\mathrm dx+\int_{0}^{3}\mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx.$$
Which claims are **necessarily** true?

$$\text{I}\ \ \mathrm f(x)\leq0\ \text{for some }x\in[1,3]\qquad
\text{II}\ \ \int_{0}^{3}\mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx\leq\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** neither &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** I and II

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**D.** Isolate the squared term:
$$\int_{0}^{3}\big(\mathrm f(x)\big)^{2}\,\mathrm dx=\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm f-\int_{0}^{3}\mathrm f=-\int_{1}^{3}\mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx.$$
The left side is an integral of a **square**, so it is $\geq0$. Therefore
$$-\int_{1}^{3}\mathrm f\geq0\;\Longrightarrow\;\int_{1}^{3}\mathrm f(x)\,\mathrm dx\leq0.$$

- **II** *is* the statement $\int_{0}^{3}\mathrm f-\int_{0}^{1}\mathrm f=\int_{1}^{3}\mathrm f\leq0$ — **true**.
- **I:** if $\mathrm f(x)>0$ **everywhere** on $[1,3]$ then $\int_{1}^{3}\mathrm f>0$, contradicting the line
  above. So $\mathrm f$ must dip to $\leq0$ somewhere on $[1,3]$ — **true**.

Both hold — **D**.

*Toolkit link (S3): the engine is "$\int(\text{square})\geq0$". Everything the identity forces flows from that
one sign fact.*
:::

## Question 14

An arithmetic sequence $T$ has first term $a$ and common difference $d$, both **non-zero integers**. Property
**P**: *for some positive integer $m$, the sum of the first $m$ terms equals the sum of the first $2m$ terms.*
(Example: $a=11,d=-2$ has P, since the first $4$ terms and first $8$ terms both sum to $32$.) Which statements
are **true**?

$$\text{I}\ \ \text{For P, it is }\textbf{sufficient}\text{ that }ad<0.\qquad
\text{II}\ \ \text{For P, it is }\textbf{necessary}\text{ that }d\text{ is even.}$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** neither &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** I and II

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**A.** First turn P into algebra. With $S_n=\tfrac n2\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$, setting $S_m=S_{2m}$ and dividing by
$m$ gives, after simplifying,
$$\boxed{\,2a+(3m-1)d=0\,}\quad\text{for some positive integer }m.$$

- **I — "$ad<0$ is sufficient":** rearrange to $3m-1=-\dfrac{2a}{d}$. For P we need this to be a **positive
  integer of the form $3m-1$** (i.e. $\equiv2\pmod 3$). Having $ad<0$ only makes $-\tfrac{2a}{d}$ positive; it
  need not be a valid $3m-1$. Counterexample $a=2,d=-1$ ($ad=-2<0$): $-\tfrac{2a}{d}=4$, but $3m-1=4$ gives
  $m=\tfrac53$, not an integer — **P fails**. So not sufficient. ✘
- **II — "$d$ even is necessary":** find P with $d$ **odd**. Take $a=-1,d=1$ and $m=1$: $2(-1)+(3-1)(1)=0$ ✔,
  and indeed $S_1=-1=S_2$. Here $d=1$ is odd, yet P holds — so $d$ even is **not** forced. ✘

Neither is true — **A**.

*Toolkit link (S3): reduce the property to one equation first, then test "sufficient" (does the hypothesis
force a valid $m$?) and "necessary" (can the property happen with the condition broken?) separately.*
:::

## Question 15

Which one is a **necessary and sufficient** condition for
$\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}\sin\!\Big(\frac{k\pi}{3}\Big)=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}$?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $n=1$ &nbsp; **B** $n$ a multiple of $3$ &nbsp; **C** $n$ a multiple of $6$ &nbsp;
**D** $n$ is $1$ more than a multiple of $3$ &nbsp; **E** $n$ is $1$ more than a multiple of $6$ &nbsp;
**F** $n$ is $1$ more than a multiple of $6$, or $2$ more than a multiple of $6$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**D.** The terms $\sin\!\big(\tfrac{k\pi}{3}\big)$ repeat with period $6$:
$$\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2},\ \tfrac{\sqrt3}{2},\ 0,\ -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2},\ -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2},\ 0,\ \dots$$
and one full block sums to $0$. So track the **running total** $S_n$ through one period:
$$S_1=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2},\quad S_2=\sqrt3,\quad S_3=\sqrt3,\quad S_4=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2},\quad S_5=0,\quad S_6=0,$$
then it repeats ($S_{n+6}=S_n$). Within each block, $S_n=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ **only** at $n=1$ and $n=4$ — both
$\equiv1\pmod 3$. Because the block sum is $0$, this pattern recurs exactly at $n=1,4,7,10,\dots$, i.e.
**$n$ is one more than a multiple of $3$**. Necessary *and* sufficient — **D**.

(Not E: $n=4$ works but is not "$1$ more than a multiple of $6$". The correct spacing is every $3$, not
every $6$.)

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
n=np.arange(1,13); S=np.cumsum(np.sin(n*np.pi/3))
fig,ax=plt.subplots(figsize=(5.0,2.8))
ax.axhline(np.sqrt(3)/2,color='crimson',ls=':',lw=1.2,label='$\\sqrt{3}/2$')
hit=np.isclose(S,np.sqrt(3)/2)
ax.plot(n,S,'-o',color='#2b6cb0',ms=4)
ax.plot(n[hit],S[hit],'o',color='#dd6b20',ms=8,label='$S_n=\\sqrt{3}/2$')
ax.set_xticks(n); ax.set_xlabel('$n$'); ax.set_ylabel('$S_n$')
ax.legend(fontsize=8,loc='lower right'); ax.set_title('Running total hits $\\sqrt{3}/2$ at $n=1,4,7,10$',fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

## Question 16

The FTC says $\dfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\Big(\int_{0}^{x}\mathrm f(t)\,\mathrm dt\Big)=\mathrm f(x)$. A
student computes $\dfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\Big(\int_{x}^{2x}t^{2}\,\mathrm dt\Big)$:

$$\begin{aligned}
&\textstyle\int_{x}^{2x}t^{2}\,\mathrm dt=\int_{0}^{2x}t^{2}\,\mathrm dt-\int_{0}^{x}t^{2}\,\mathrm dt &&\text{(I)}\\
&\textstyle\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\!\int_{0}^{x}t^{2}\,\mathrm dt=x^{2} &&\text{(II)}\\
&\textstyle\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\!\int_{0}^{2x}t^{2}\,\mathrm dt=(2x)^{2}=4x^{2} &&\text{(III)}\\
&\textstyle\tfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\!\int_{x}^{2x}t^{2}\,\mathrm dt=4x^{2}-x^{2} &&\text{(IV)}\\
&\textstyle=3x^{2} &&\text{(V)}
\end{aligned}$$

Which best describes the calculation?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** completely correct &nbsp; **B** first error line (I) &nbsp; **C** line (II) &nbsp;
**D** line (III) &nbsp; **E** line (IV) &nbsp; **F** line (V)

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**D.** Line (I) (splitting the integral) is fine, and line (II) is a correct FTC application. The error is at
**line (III)**: the upper limit is $2x$, not $x$, so the FTC needs the **chain rule**:
$$\frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dx}\int_{0}^{2x}t^{2}\,\mathrm dt=(2x)^{2}\cdot\frac{\mathrm d(2x)}{\mathrm dx}=(2x)^{2}\cdot2=8x^{2},$$
not $4x^{2}$. The student forgot the "$\times2$".

**Check by direct integration:** $\int_{x}^{2x}t^{2}\,\mathrm dt=\big[\tfrac{t^{3}}{3}\big]_{x}^{2x}=\tfrac{8x^{3}-x^{3}}{3}=\tfrac{7x^{3}}{3}$,
so the true derivative is $7x^{2}$ — with the correction, $8x^{2}-x^{2}=7x^{2}$ ✔. The student's $3x^{2}$ is
wrong, and the first slip is at (III).

*Toolkit link (S7): the FTC only reads off "$\mathrm f(\text{upper limit})$" when the upper limit is exactly
$x$. Any other upper limit $g(x)$ carries a $\times g'(x)$.*
:::

## Question 17

A set of six **distinct** integers is split into two sets of three. The first set has mean $10$ and median
$8$; the second has mean $12$ and median $9$. What is the smallest possible **range** of the six integers?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $8$ &nbsp; **B** $10$ &nbsp; **C** $11$ &nbsp; **D** $12$ &nbsp; **E** $14$ &nbsp; **F** $15$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**E.** Write the sets as $\{a,8,b\}$ with $a<8<b$ and $\{c,9,d\}$ with $c<9<d$.

- Mean $10$ (sum $30$) gives $a+b=22$; mean $12$ (sum $36$) gives $c+d=27$.
- To shrink the range we want the **maximum small** and the **minimum large**. The two largest are $b=22-a$
  and $d=27-c$; the two smallest are $a$ and $c$.

Push the small ends up: $a\leq7$ and $c\leq7$ (both must stay below their medians, and $8$ is already used).
The binding constraint is $d=27-c\geq27-7=20$, so the maximum is **at least $20$**, achieved with $c=7$. With
$c=7$ the value $7$ is taken, so $a\leq6$; take $a=6,b=16$. Then the smallest value is $6$.
$$\{6,8,16\}\ \text{(mean }10,\text{ median }8)\quad\{7,9,20\}\ \text{(mean }12,\text{ median }9)$$
All six are distinct and the range is $20-6=14$. No arrangement beats this, so the smallest range is **14**.

*Any attempt to reach $19$ as the maximum needs $c=8$, but $8$ is already the first median — so $20$ is
forced, and $14$ is the best possible.*
:::

## Question 18

$\mathrm f(x)=ax^{3}+bx^{2}+cx+d$ and $\mathrm g(x)=px^{3}+qx^{2}+rx+s$ are cubics. If $\mathrm f(x)-\mathrm
g(x)>0$ for **every** real $x$, which is/are **necessarily** true?

$$\text{I}\ \ a>p\qquad \text{II}\ \ \text{if }b=q\text{ then }c=r\qquad \text{III}\ \ d>s$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none &nbsp; **B** I only &nbsp; **C** II only &nbsp; **D** III only &nbsp;
**E** I and II &nbsp; **F** I and III &nbsp; **G** II and III &nbsp; **H** I, II and III

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**G.** Let $h(x)=\mathrm f(x)-\mathrm g(x)=(a-p)x^{3}+(b-q)x^{2}+(c-r)x+(d-s)$, and use that $h(x)>0$ for all
real $x$.

- **Degree first:** a genuine cubic ($a-p\neq0$) runs to $-\infty$ on one side, so it cannot stay positive.
  Hence $a-p=0$, i.e. $a=p$. So **I ($a>p$) is false** — it is "$=$", not "$>$".
- With $a=p$, $h$ is at most quadratic: $(b-q)x^{2}+(c-r)x+(d-s)>0$ for all $x$.
- **III ($d>s$): true.** Put $x=0$: $h(0)=d-s>0$.
- **II: true.** *If* $b=q$, then $h$ collapses to the linear $(c-r)x+(d-s)$. A non-constant line cannot stay
  positive for all $x$, so we must have $c-r=0$, i.e. $c=r$. The implication "$b=q\Rightarrow c=r$" holds.

So II and III are forced but I is not — **G**.

*Toolkit link (S1/S2): "positive for all $x$" is a strong hypothesis — it kills odd leading terms, pins the
value at $0$, and forces the linear coefficient to vanish once the quadratic term is gone.*
:::

## Question 19

Nine people sit in a $3\times3$ grid, one per square; **neighbours** share a side. Each is a truth-teller
(always tells the truth) or a liar (always lies). Every person says: *"My neighbours are all liars."* What are
the **smallest** and **largest** numbers who could be telling the truth?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $1,4$ &nbsp; **B** $2,4$ &nbsp; **C** $2,5$ &nbsp; **D** $3,4$ &nbsp; **E** $3,5$ &nbsp;
**F** $4,4$ &nbsp; **G** $4,5$ &nbsp; **H** $5,5$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**E.** Translate the statement for each type:

- A **truth-teller (T)** speaks truly, so *all* their neighbours really are liars — **no two T's are adjacent**.
- A **liar (L)** speaks falsely, so it is **not** true that all their neighbours are liars — **every L has at
  least one T neighbour**.

Together: the truth-tellers form a set that is **independent** (no two adjacent) **and dominating** (every
other cell touches one). We want the smallest and largest such set.

- **Smallest $=3$.** Fewer than $3$ cannot dominate all nine (the centre reaches only $4$ of the $8$ others,
  leaving corners uncovered). Three suffice, e.g. T at the shaded cells below (top-left, mid-right,
  bottom-mid): every empty cell touches a T and no two T's are adjacent.
- **Largest $=5$.** The most independent cells in a $3\times3$ grid is the checkerboard $\{$four corners $+$
  centre$\}=5$, and every edge-cell touches one of them — independent *and* dominating.

So the answer is $3$ and $5$ — **E**.

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
def draw(ax,T,title):
    for i in range(4):
        ax.plot([0,3],[i,i],color='0.3',lw=1); ax.plot([i,i],[0,3],color='0.3',lw=1)
    for (r,c) in T:   # r row from top (0..2), c col (0..2)
        ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((c,2-r),1,1,color='#bcd3ef'))
        ax.text(c+0.5,2-r+0.5,'T',ha='center',va='center',fontsize=13,weight='bold',color='#1f3864')
    for r in range(3):
        for c in range(3):
            if (r,c) not in T:
                ax.text(c+0.5,2-r+0.5,'L',ha='center',va='center',fontsize=12,color='0.5')
    ax.set_xlim(-.2,3.2); ax.set_ylim(-.2,3.2); ax.set_aspect('equal'); ax.axis('off')
    ax.set_title(title,fontsize=9)
fig,axes=plt.subplots(1,2,figsize=(6.2,3.2))
draw(axes[0],{(0,0),(1,2),(2,1)},'Smallest: 3 truth-tellers')
draw(axes[1],{(0,0),(0,2),(1,1),(2,0),(2,2)},'Largest: 5 truth-tellers')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```
:::

## Question 20

$x$ is a real number and $\mathrm f$ is a function. Given that **exactly one** of the following is true, which
one is it?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $x\geq0$ only if $\mathrm f(x)<0$ &nbsp; **B** $x<0$ if $\mathrm f(x)\geq0$ &nbsp;
**C** $x\geq0$ only if $\mathrm f(x)\geq0$ &nbsp; **D** $\mathrm f(x)<0$ if $x<0$ &nbsp;
**E** $\mathrm f(x)\geq0$ only if $x\geq0$ &nbsp; **F** $\mathrm f(x)\geq0$ if and only if $x<0$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution
**C.** Write $p:\ x\geq0$ and $q:\ \mathrm f(x)\geq0$, and translate each option ("$P$ only if $Q$" is
$P\Rightarrow Q$; "$P$ if $Q$" is $Q\Rightarrow P$):

$$\text{A}:p\Rightarrow\neg q,\quad \text{B}:q\Rightarrow\neg p,\quad \text{C}:p\Rightarrow q,\quad
\text{D}:\neg p\Rightarrow\neg q,\quad \text{E}:q\Rightarrow p,\quad \text{F}:q\Leftrightarrow\neg p.$$

Now spot the **equivalent pairs**:
$$\text{A}\equiv\text{B}\ (\text{both }\neg p\vee\neg q),\qquad \text{D}\equiv\text{E}\ (\text{both }p\vee\neg q).$$
Members of a pair always share the same truth value, so if the unique true statement were A, B, D or E, its
partner would be true too — **two** true statements, contradicting "exactly one". The single true one must
therefore be **C or F**.

Rule out **F**: if F were the only true one, then C would be false, meaning $x\geq0$ **and** $\mathrm f(x)<0$
— but that very situation makes A ($x\geq0\Rightarrow\mathrm f(x)<0$) **true**, giving a second true statement.
Contradiction. So the exactly-one-true statement is **C**.

*Toolkit link (S2): the fast route is recognising the two equivalent pairs; whatever is uniquely true has to
be one of the un-paired statements, C or F.*
:::
